query: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, low-percentage of an oxyphilic dopant (e.g., Sn) into the nearly equiatomic multi-element automotive alloy catalyst will improve both its activity and durability under transient, low‐temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust conditions, while retaining low platinum-group metal use.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst consisting of nearly equiatomic ratios of Pt along with base metals such as Ni, Fe, Co, and Cu.
generation.intervention: Doping the catalyst with a small, optimized concentration of tin (Sn) during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Operation under transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions with exposure to H2O and NO, including stress from thermal aging and high mileage cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: The incorporation of Sn modifies the local coordination environment at the active sites, particularly around Pt atoms, enhancing oxyphilicity and electron transfer between adjacent atoms.
generation.mechanism: Sn acts as an oxyphilic element to promote the adsorption of OH− species and facilitates the removal of poisoning intermediates (e.g., CO), thereby lowering oxidation energy barriers and maintaining moderate binding of key reaction intermediates. This electron structure modulation mitigates catalyst deactivation mechanisms during prolonged thermal and chemical stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Sn-doped catalyst will exhibit lower overpotentials, enhanced reaction rates, and superior resistance to deactivation (i.e., less sintering and poisoning) compared to the untreated catalyst under identical exhaust conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (activity, overpotential, durability) of the untreated multi-element alloy catalyst under the same low-temperature, transient exhaust conditions with H2O and NO exposure.
generation.boundary: Benefits are expected within the optimized dopant concentration and under exhaust conditions mimicking typical transient low-temperature operation; performance under extreme or prolonged exposure beyond tested aging cycles remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentration of Sn and its long-term effects under real-world automotive conditions require further empirical tuning; additional variables such as interactions with other alloy elements may influence the effectiveness of the doping strategy.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the catalyst: one as the baseline multi-element alloy and one doped with the optimized amount of Sn. Expose each batch to simulated transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions that include periodic H2O and NO exposure and accelerated thermal aging cycles (to mimic high mileage). Measure catalytic performance and stability over time.
measurements: Catalytic conversion rates (e.g., reaction kinetics, onset temperatures)
Overpotential values required for target reactions
Surface composition and oxidation state analysis via XPS
Particle size distribution and phase homogeneity (via TEM and XRD) before and after aging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in both activity (e.g., lower overpotential or enhanced reaction rate) and durability (i.e., greater retention of activity and structural stability) relative to the untreated catalyst, the hypothesis will be refuted.

As the first order of approximation, we introduced a doping Co/Ni/Bi/Sn atom onto Pt(111) surface to evaluate the individual contribution from each kind of element in HEASA-Pt (Supplementary Fig. 2). Co and Bi have been reported to promote electron transfer in catalysts, lowering the oxidation energy barrier of *CO and facilitating the MOR,. Ni and Sn can act as oxyphilic elements to enhance the adsorption of OH−, thereby accelerating the oxidation of *CO and improving the anti-CO poisoning ability of catalysts,. The effects of the alloying elements could be separated into two categories. On the one hand, modification of the coordination environment around Pt influences its reactivity. As shown in Fig. 1b, doping with a Bi or Sn atom weakened CO binding on adjacent Pt sites, suppressing CO poisoning, which is a well-known degradation mechanism of Pt-based MOR catalysts.
